extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature (undergraduate/introductory to classical literary theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing or composing epic and tragic literature using Aristotelian principles (genre definitions, mimesis, plot, character, catharsis, unities, etc.). Useful as a checklist for close reading, criticism, or creative composition informed by Poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and generic attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor definitions of literary genres in exemplary works and authors; distinguish genres by their characteristic traits (e.g., Aristotle considered Sophocles best of tragedians; Homeric epics as exemplar of epic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exemplary texts as prototypes; note Aristotle's claim that genres may originate in pairs (e.g., Margites ~ comic drama vs. Iliad/Odyssey ~ tragedy). When distinguishing epic vs. tragedy, prefer epic's multiplicity of plots vs. tragedy's compressed single plot. Beware historical contestability (other tragedians survived) and later forms (tragi-comedy, satire) which blur Aristotelian binaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis / Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: All literature is an art of imitation (mimesis); literature imitates life and can inspire audiences to imitate what they read/see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the moral/social effects of imitation: epic can exemplify good behavior; comedy imitates 'low characters' (ludicrous or ugly but not destructively evil) and, according to Aristotle, discourages imitation by making the behavior laughable. Evaluate works by how they represent characters and actions and the likely social influence of that imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should imitate action that is serious, complete, and of an appropriate magnitude (neither trivial nor too vast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the seriousness and scale of action fit the genre and produce believable stakes; avoid trivializing tragedy or overextending action beyond what can be cohesively represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature's function (katharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy evokes pity and fear to cleanse (katharsis) the mind of dangerous natural tendencies (e.g., overgrown pride), restoring the health of the polis when experienced communally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating tragedy, ask whether the plot and staging produce pity and fear and whether that emotional purging is intellectually or socially coherent; consider the communal/social function of that catharsis in the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic characters are judged by thought and character; proper characters should have goodness (moral sense), appropriateness to social mores, truth to life (probability in small details), and consistency (not disturbingly divided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters for moral disposition, social fit, lifelike detail, and psychological consistency. Anti-patterns include implausible character actions, moral incoherence, or split/nonsensical characterization that breaks audience plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-components of dramatic theater (six parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedies have six parts: plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle (special effects), and song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these six parts as analytic categories when assessing drama: prioritize plot as primary, but weigh diction (language), thought (ideas/reasoning), spectacle (visual impact), song (musical elements), and character. Note Aristotle's ranking emphasizes plot as the 'first principle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature and human nature (plot as first principle, hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our qualities are determined by character, but happiness/wretchedness by actions. Great literature shows actions at crucial moments; the first principle of drama is plot. A perfect tragedy imitates complex actions that excite pity and fear and lead a fundamentally good/just person to misfortune by error of judgment or frailty (hamartia/tragic imbalance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plots for their centrality, causal integrity, and how well they dramatize decisive actions; identify the protagonist's error or imbalance producing downfall rather than simple moral depravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of a work of literature (unities of form and time)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy's plot should have a beginning, middle, and end (completeness) and be of appropriate size to be 'easily embraced in one view' or by memory; the work should move a character from calamity to good fortune or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the narrative feels organically whole—sized and structured so its arc is graspable; critique 'episodic' plots that move incident-to-incident without probable cause (an anti-pattern, though modernism sometimes tests this boundary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot should be unified: centered around a single action or chain of causally linked events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for causal coherence and focus—avoid digressions or multiple unrelated plotlines unless they clearly serve a unified action or purpose; be wary of circular/tautological definitions but use unity as an organizing ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs. history — the 'truth' problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Poet and historian differ: the historian relates what happened, while the poet may relate what may or might have happened; poets are not merely liars but generalizers about possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging fictional works, emphasize their capacity to reveal general truths or possibilities rather than factual accuracy. Use this distinction to defend imaginative truth against charges of 'lying.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs. complex plots (peripeteia and anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex plot includes reversal of expectations (peripeteia) and/or recognition (anagnorisis), usually producing powerful audience effects; Aristotle divides dramatic action into complication and unraveling, with these moments often occurring near the end (e.g., Oedipus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and evaluate structural devices like reversal and recognition; they increase plot complexity and emotional impact. In contrast, simple plots lack these features and have a straightforward causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature and the 'agon' (double thread)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle saw works as patterns of struggle (agon) between opposed forces; tragedy and epic may develop collisions between opposing character types and often contain a 'double thread'—concern for two groups with opposite ends (e.g., Odysseus vs. the suitors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze opposing forces, dual plot-threads, or binary conflicts that structure the narrative; this principle helps explain thematic tension and the interplay of competing aims or moral orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle / Special Effects vs. tragic/comic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate works that move audiences by thoughtful emotional processes from those that shock via spectacle (taboo scenes, explicit violence or sex). Spectacle can move emotion but is distinct from the primarily intellectual/emotional processes Aristotle favors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique reliance on spectacle as a substitute for proper tragic or comic construction; consider examples (modern horror films like Halloween) that use shock—ask whether spectacle serves or supplants character, plot, and catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition and the individual talent (respect for received framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great art derives from tradition, and poets adapting legends must not 'destroy the framework of the received legends'; there is tension between innovation and preserving essential elements of inherited myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting traditional material, assess whether changes violate the essential framework of the source (per Aristotle) or whether innovation is justified. Consider religious/social constraints in the original cultural context as limits on alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry, Inspiration and Madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle allows craft in poetry but holds that truly great poets are either specially gifted (able to imitate any character) or mad (unable to maintain their own characters); poets combine skill and exceptional temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetic talent as both technical craft and exceptional capacity; avoid reducing poetic creation solely to divine madness or mere technique—look for evidence of craftful imitation and extraordinary imaginative power.
